archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (run-first, turnover-sunk)
archetype.definition: A below-average team with a real ground game and a disciplined, clock-eating identity whose 2-5 mark is dragged a notch further down by the league's worst turnover margin and a broken passing attack.

report.headline: A good run game buried by giveaways and a passing offense that can't function.
report.take:
The Colts have a clear identity. They lean on Jonathan Taylor, who has 140 carries, run the ball efficiently enough to rank 4th in rush EPA, hold the ball for the 5th-most time per game, and commit the fewest penalties in the league. That is the profile of a team that should grind out close games. The problem is the other half of the offense. Passing EPA sits 30th, the line has allowed 19 sacks, and the offense as a whole ranks 27th in EPA. Last season this same franchise had the 7th-best offense by EPA, so this isn't a long-standing ceiling. Something in the passing game has broken in 2026, and Daniel Jones has started every week through it.

The record is mostly a turnover story. Indianapolis has given the ball away 12 times and taken it away 3 times, a minus-9 margin that ranks dead last per game. Its point differential implies 3.2 wins rather than 2, and it has won only a quarter of its one-score games. The Week 6 home loss to Tennessee, a 6.5-point favorite against the 31st-ranked offense, shows it plainly: three giveaways and six sacks allowed against a team it outgained. Some of this will regress. A team this clean with penalties isn't usually this sloppy with the football.

The defense is better than the points allowed suggest, but it has a structural hole. It ranks 10th in success rate allowed and 4th on third downs, so it gets stops in rhythm. It also ranks 31st in pressure rate, 28th in rush EPA allowed and 30th in takeaways. Those last three are linked: without pressure there are few hurried throws, so few interceptions. The low takeaway count is partly bad luck and partly the pass rush. The schedule context cuts both ways. Four of the five losses came to Baltimore, Kansas City, Pittsburgh and Minnesota, but the two wins came against Houston and Washington, defenses that now rank 24th and 25th.

Where this goes depends on the passing game holding together through injuries. Tyler Warren, the starting tight end and third in targets, is out. Alec Pierce is on IR. Sauce Gardner is out at corner and Justin Walley is questionable. The back half of the schedule is soft: Miami, Houston, Philadelphia, Tennessee and a Dallas defense ranked 30th. A run-first team that stops turning it over could stack wins there. A division title would take more than that, and the efficiency numbers don't promise it.

strengths.title: An efficient, physical run game
strengths.body: Rush EPA ranks 4th and run success 10th, with Taylor carrying most of the load and a line that wins in short yardage. It holds up against good fronts: they ran for 154 yards against Minnesota's top-ranked defense. Run EPA is a stable trait for a line this disciplined, so expect it to last, though game script can take it away when they fall behind.

strengths.title: Discipline and ball control
strengths.body: Fewest penalties per game in the league, 3rd-fewest line penalties, and the 5th-most time of possession. This is a coached trait rather than variance, and it keeps games short and close. That helps explain why they cover more often than their record suggests.

strengths.title: Third-down defense gets off the field
strengths.body: Opponents convert only 30% of third downs, 4th-best, and success rate allowed ranks 10th. The unit wins on structure and tackling position more than with a pass rush. It's a real skill, but it is exposed when offenses stay on schedule with the run.

concerns.title: Passing offense near the bottom
concerns.body: Pass EPA ranks 30th, the sack rate 23rd, and the offense passes less than expected. That reads as a staff hiding the quarterback rather than a run-heavy philosophy choice. It is a sharp fall from an offense that ranked 7th in EPA last year. With Warren and Pierce out, the receiving corps thins further, so a quick fix is unlikely.

concerns.title: Worst turnover margin in football
concerns.body: Twelve giveaways against three takeaways have cost them roughly a win relative to their point differential. The giveaway side should regress toward normal for a disciplined team. The takeaway side is partly structural, because the pass rush doesn't force mistakes.

concerns.title: No pass rush, soft against the run
concerns.body: Pressure rate ranks 31st and rush EPA allowed 28th, so the defense can be moved on the ground and gives quarterbacks clean pockets. Losing Gardner at corner removes the coverage that covered for the missing rush. That makes this the most likely flaw to get worse before it improves.

trend.note: The offense scored 30 twice in the first four weeks, then 22, 20 and 10 as the passing game cratered and the sacks piled up. Three straight losses include the giveaway-filled home defeat to Tennessee.

nextGame.headline: Colts' best weapon runs straight into Jacksonville's strength
nextGame.body:
This is a bad stylistic draw. Indianapolis wants to run, and Jacksonville ranks 4th in rush EPA allowed, 3rd in explosive runs allowed, and has been the stingiest defense in the league against lead backs. If Taylor is bottled up, Jones has to throw from behind against a pass rush ranked 8th in pressure rate, the exact situation where this offense has turned it over. The opening is downfield: the Jaguars are the best team in football against short throws but 29th on deep passes, and they have struggled with WR1s and WR3s. On the other side, Trevor Lawrence leads a passing offense ranked 4th in EPA against a Colts defense that can't pressure him. The Book makes Jacksonville a 7.5-point favorite. The early forecast flags possible thunderstorms, but the wind looks manageable.

Availability tilts toward Jacksonville. The Colts are without Gardner, their top corner, and Warren, their starting tight end. Walley is questionable at corner, and two backup linebackers are out. Jacksonville has lost starting right tackle Anton Harrison to a torn ACL, which is a real opening. Indianapolis's 31st-ranked pressure rate makes it hard to cash in on, though. Jaguars safety Antonio Johnson and corner Montaric Brown are questionable, which could thin the secondary the Colts need to attack deep.

waysToWin.title: Take shots at Jacksonville's deep coverage
waysToWin.body: The Jaguars allow almost nothing short but rank 29th in deep-pass EPA and 29th against WR1s. Josh Downs and Keenan Allen draw the volume, and a handful of completions downfield could flip a game the run can't win. It needs clean protection, so play-action off the run threat is the likely vehicle.

waysToWin.title: Shorten the game, win on third down
waysToWin.body: The Colts' formula is long drives, no penalties and third-down stops, and Jacksonville is a middle-of-the-pack team on flags. Keeping possessions few and the score close puts pressure on the Jaguars late. The Colts' 4th-ranked third-down defense is the piece that makes that script possible.

waysToWin.title: Attack the Harrison-less right side
waysToWin.body: Jacksonville lost a 92%-snap starting tackle. Even a weak rush can find a mismatch against a replacement, and a couple of drive-killing sacks or a strip would be the turnover luck this team is overdue for.

waysToLose.title: Run game stalls, Jones throws into pressure
waysToLose.body: Jacksonville's run defense is elite against exactly the role Taylor fills. Long-yardage passing against an 8th-ranked pressure rate is where this line, 26th in sacks allowed, gives up drive-enders and turnovers. The Tennessee loss showed how fast that snowballs.

waysToLose.title: Lawrence picks apart a thin secondary
waysToLose.body: A top-4 passing offense facing no pressure and no Gardner is the worst matchup on the board. The Colts' trouble with WR3s and tight ends gives Jacksonville easy completions to keep drives alive.

waysToLose.title: Turnover margin breaks the wrong way again
waysToLose.body: Jacksonville is 5th in turnover margin per game, and Indianapolis is last. Another multi-giveaway game makes a 7.5-point spread easy to cover.

nextGame.watch: Whether the Colts throw downfield on early downs. Jacksonville takes away everything short and the run, so the deep ball is the only place it bleeds.

restOfSeason.body:
The turnover margin is the most likely thing to improve. A team this clean with penalties and this run-heavy shouldn't keep giving the ball away at this rate, and that alone should turn some close losses into wins. The remaining schedule helps too, with Miami, Houston, Philadelphia, Tennessee and a 30th-ranked Dallas defense still ahead. What won't regress on its own is the passing game, which ranks 30th and is losing pieces, or a pass rush ranked 31st that keeps takeaways scarce.

The realistic picture is a team that wins the soft games it controls on the ground and loses to the better ones: Jacksonville twice, Cincinnati and Cleveland. That lands somewhere in the 6-8 win range, short of the division unless the Jaguars fade. If Warren and Gardner return healthy and the passing offense climbs back toward last year's level, there's upside. If the giveaways continue, this becomes a high draft pick.
swingFactors: Turnover regression on the giveaway side
Passing offense health (Warren, Pierce) and protection
Gardner's return to a pass defense with no rush

confidence.note: Seven games, a stable QB and clear efficiency signals, but turnover luck and key injuries add noise.
